title: The next big thing in hydrogen could be underground
gist: Naturally occurring 'geologic hydrogen' is overtaking electrolyzer- and carbon-capture-based clean hydrogen as the field's momentum leader, with companies like HyTerra finding gas up to 96% hydrogen concentration and Koloma raising over $400 million to prospect the US Midcontinent Rift, though storage and transport of the light, hard-to-contain gas remains unsolved.

themes.theme: Geologic Hydrogen Gains Momentum Over Electrolysis and CCS

insights.claim: Electrolyzer-based and carbon-capture-abated approaches to clean hydrogen have both struggled to gain ground primarily due to high cost, opening room for geologic (naturally occurring) hydrogen to become the field's new momentum leader.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Signals a possible capital-allocation shift within the clean-hydrogen sector away from electrolysis/CCS plays toward geologic-hydrogen prospecting and stimulation companies.
insights.quote: both those methods have struggled to gain ground, largely because of their high cost. Lately, there’s been momentum in a new field: geologic hydrogen.
insights.locator: If you’d asked me a few years ago

insights.claim: The US Midcontinent Rift, a roughly billion-year-old crustal split running from Kansas to Michigan, is a hydrogen hotspot because it left behind iron-rich rock that readily reacts with water to generate hydrogen.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, mappable US geologic corridor as the near-term exploration target for geologic-hydrogen companies.
insights.locator: One hot spot is the Midwest

insights.claim: HyTerra, an Australian company prospecting across Nebraska and Kansas, has already found gas samples with hydrogen concentrations up to 96%.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-pure hydrogen concentration result is an early proof point that natural accumulations of commercially relevant purity exist in the Midcontinent Rift region.
insights.quote: it’s already found samples of gas with hydrogen concentrations up to 96%

insights.claim: Researchers examining boreholes at a mine in northern Ontario found each one released about eight kilograms of hydrogen per year, and with more than 14,000 boreholes at that single site, the aggregate capture potential from existing mine infrastructure is substantial.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Suggests existing mining infrastructure could be repurposed for hydrogen capture without new drilling, a lower-capex pathway worth tracking.
insights.quote: each one released eight kilograms of hydrogen per year
insights.locator: Researchers examined a few dozen boreholes

insights.claim: Koloma is one of the most capitalized companies in the geologic-hydrogen space, with total funding over $400 million, and is prospecting in the same Midwest Midcontinent Rift region as HyTerra.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A $400M+ funding level for a single geologic-hydrogen prospector is a concrete benchmark for how much institutional capital already believes in this sub-sector.
insights.quote: one of the most capitalized companies in the space with total funding over $400 million
insights.locator: Koloma, one of the most capitalized companies

themes.theme: Engineered 'Stimulated' Hydrogen as a Second Business Model

insights.claim: Beyond hunting for natural hydrogen accumulations, a second business model -- 'stimulated geologic hydrogen' -- involves injecting water, a catalyst, or another reaction trigger into rock formations that have favorable conditions but no accumulated resource, to kick-start hydrogen production on demand.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Defines a distinct, engineered-production sub-category within geologic hydrogen that doesn't depend on finding pre-existing gas accumulations -- potentially a larger addressable resource base.
insights.locator: Rather than hunt for a natural source

insights.claim: Vema Hydrogen, a Texas-based company, is testing stimulated hydrogen production by drilling wells and injecting water and catalysts in Quebec, with plans to begin full-scale production in 2028.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete commercialization timeline (2028) for the stimulated-hydrogen approach to benchmark against.
insights.locator: Vema Hydrogen is a Texas-based company

insights.claim: Eden GeoPower uses electricity to create fracture networks in rock, opening more pathways for water to infiltrate and drive hydrogen-generating reactions, with potential crossover applications in enhanced geothermal projects.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Highlights a technology (electrically induced fracturing) with dual applicability to both geologic hydrogen and enhanced geothermal, a potential platform play.
insights.locator: Other companies are tackling different aspects

insights.claim: Even if geologic hydrogen production scales, hydrogen's small molecular weight makes it notoriously difficult to move and store, requiring either large storage volumes or cryogenic liquefaction at super-low temperatures.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Storage/transport logistics remain an unresolved bottleneck that could cap the economic upside of geologic-hydrogen discoveries regardless of how much gas is found.
insights.quote: Hydrogen is notoriously difficult to move around and store, requiring either a lot of space or super-low temperatures to force the gas to become liquid.
insights.locator: There are still a ton of unanswered questions here
